details: identities reproduced across two runs: 5 signals, 5 representations

results.title: Information preservation: raw → scalar vs raw → (A, E, C) | U
results.hypothesis: Compressing an observation into a single scalar discards provenance, method, temporal, quality, context, and uncertainty information that a reviewer needs in order to interpret it.
results.method: Enumerate recoverable facts from each raw observation, then check which of those facts are recoverable from the 1:3 representation and from a scalar mean of response positions. Compare counts.

measures.label: facts enumerated from the raw observations
facts recoverable from (A, E, C) | U
measures.note: recoverability is checked by set membership against the primitive values recorded in the representation

measures.label: facts recoverable from the scalar compression
measures.note: the scalar is 0.7500 (mean of 5 positions) plus an observation count

measures.label: scalar value
measures.note: shown to make the compression concrete; it is not stored anywhere in the system

observations: Each observation contributes 42 recoverable facts on average.

Not every enumerated fact is recoverable, and the exceptions are recorded rather than hidden: source.label. The human-readable source label is a display convenience; the representation keeps the stable source reference instead.

Scalar compression retains the aggregate reading and the count, but none of the enumerated facts: provenance, method version, timestamps, quality metadata, context fields, and uncertainty are all unrecoverable from it.
The (A, E, C) | U representation retains the raw response alongside its interpretation policy, so a reviewer can recompute the reading rather than trust it.
limitations: Fact counts are a proxy for information content: they measure the recoverability of enumerated facts, not the semantic value of the information.
The enumeration is authored by this project; a different enumeration would change the percentages while leaving the ordering (1:3 ≫ scalar) unchanged.
This experiment says nothing about whether the facts are the *right* facts to record for career assessment.

results.title: Provenance recovery with and without the E facet
results.hypothesis: Removing the evidence facet destroys a reviewer’s ability to establish source, method, timestamp, version, and evidence quality.
results.method: Render every representation twice (E present, E restricted) and count how many of six provenance questions the rendered output can answer.

measures.label: provenance recovery rate with E present
provenance recovery rate with E restricted
weakest provenance question
measures.value: Where did this observation come from?
measures.note: the question least often answerable from a full render

observations: With E present, every provenance question is answerable, including the method’s declared limitations.
With E restricted, the questions that remain answerable are: method, timestamp. Where a question survives restriction it is because another facet leaked the answer, not because E is unnecessary.

The observed leakage is informative: the assessment facet carries the observation timestamp, and uncertainty notes quote the collection method in their detail text. Provenance therefore cannot be "removed" by hiding one facet — it has to be replaced by an explicit statement of what is unknown.

The residual (what survives restriction) is exactly the part of a claim that can be copied out of the system and still look authoritative — which is why provenance is a first-class facet rather than a UI detail.
limitations: The questions are authored by this project; a different question set would produce different rates.
The renderer is the system’s own reader: a reviewer reading raw JSON might recover more or less.
This measures recoverability from the representation, not whether a human reviewer actually reads the evidence.

results.title: Context dependence with the assessment held constant
results.hypothesis: Interpretation that is legitimately context-dependent must change when C changes while A is held constant, and the change must be explicit rather than silent.
results.method: Build three fixtures with identical responses and progressively thinner context, map each to pathways through the real capability, and compare requirement statuses, uncertainty codes, and pathway restrictions.

measures.label: assessment facet identical across context variants
requirement statuses that changed to "undetermined" when context was removed
new uncertainty codes when context was removed

observations: context declared: supported 13, gap 0, conflicting 0, undetermined 27
context thinned: supported 5, gap 0, conflicting 0, undetermined 35
context removed: supported 5, gap 0, conflicting 0, undetermined 35
Holding A constant while changing C changes what the mapping is willing to say: requirements move to "undetermined" and additional uncertainty is recorded.
The mapping never silently absorbs the context change: it reports the change through uncertainty notes, requirement rationales, and pathway restrictions.
limitations: The variants are synthetic context edits, not observed changes in a person’s situation.
Only the pathway mapping is measured; other transformations (for example model-assisted explanation) are not exercised here.
A finding that context matters for these items does not generalise to all career constructs.

results.title: Temporal comparison with assessment, evidence, and context tracked separately
results.hypothesis: An unchanged reading across two sittings is not the same as an unchanged observation: evidence and context move independently, and the representation must show that separately.
results.method: Capture and decompose the same item set twice with a fixed clock step, then compare the assessment reading, the evidence timestamps, the context delta, and the uncertainty codes for each item pair.

measures.label: pairs with a changed assessment reading
pairs where the scalar view would report "no change"
measures.note: a scalar comparison sees only the reading, not the evidence or context that moved

measures.label: pairs with a later evidence timestamp

observations: Assessment readings changed in 0 of 5 pairs, while the evidence timestamps moved in 5 and the context changed in 5.
The three dimensions are tracked separately, so "the answer did not change but the situation did" is a representable state rather than an invisible one.
A re-assessment decision can therefore cite the temporal and contextual evidence rather than the reading alone — and the decision itself remains the user’s.
limitations: The fixture’s second sitting reuses the same responses; this measures representation behaviour, not test–retest reliability of any instrument.
Two sittings cannot establish temporal stability; the experiment is a mechanism check, not a reliability study.
The instrument is unvalidated (see uncertainty notes), so no psychometric claim is made from these numbers.
